newsitem.title: UK: Golf-Australia's Elkington sees Woods win at British Open.
newsitem.headline: Golf-Australia's Elkington sees Woods win at British Open.

text.p: Steve Elkington set the Tiger Woods ball rolling at the British Open on Monday, saying the American probably won't even notice Royal Troon's bunkers "even if a guy is lying in there dead."

The Australian winner of the Doral Open and the prestigious Players Championship on the U.S. Tour this year said he regarded Woods as the favourite this week following his seventh victory in 10 months as a pro at the Western Open.
"When he does well, he comes right back out and does well again," Elkington said of the 21-year-old American phenomenon and world number one.
Some bookmakers make Woods favourite at as low as 5-1, the shortest odds quoted about any player at the start of the championship for over 20 years.
But Elkington said the combination of Troon's unpredictable rough and possible severe winds could unsettle Woods.
"He hits a high ball so he could have trouble controlling it in the wind. But he's probably been practising a low punch shot and most likely he's got it down pat by now."

Woods ran away with the U.S. Masters by 12 shots in April on the wide fairways at Augusta, but had more trouble with the narrow fairways and thick, clingy rough at the Congressional Club in Washington last month. He tied for 19th there.
Elkington, who played Troon last week, said its rough was not as thick as Congressional's, but more unpredictable.

"You have an option here. You can try to play a full shot out or you can just chip out sideways. You can't be sure what will happen. At Congressional, you knew you could only chip out. There was no option.
"Give a player an option and that gives him a chance to screw up," he said.
Elkington said as Troon is an old course, the bunkers are not far enough out from the tees to bother Woods.
"So if Tiger can hit it 350 yards into the fairways, good luck to him. He should win," the Australian added.
Elkington, who is second to Woods on the U.S. money list, feels very well-prepared for this week following his success on the U.S. Tour this year.
" I didn't play much late last year because I was getting ready for the birth of our second child in February. But I practised a lot.
"I was surprised to win those two titles and after that I felt I could beat anybody. All the hard work had paid off and I had a decent Masters and a decent U.S. Open as well," he said.
Elkington said he regarded Troon as the best conditioned Open venue he has seen.
"It seems very fair," he said. "The bunkers are not too deep and you can hit a good shot out of them. They are not deep like St Andrews' bunkers."
For all his success on the U.S. Tour, Elkington is best known in Britain for his playoff victory over local hero Colin Montgomerie in the 1995 PGA championship.
Montgomerie's father James is the secretary at Royal Troon and his son has played here since he was a boy.
"I told his father that if I don't win here, I hope Colin does. He deserves it," Elkington said.
